lessons.title: The ESOP Pool Shuffle: Why Pool Size Is Settled Before the Round

children.text: The last lesson ended with Meera at 24.00% after a clean 25% round. Now read the rest of the term sheet. One line, buried under governance: "The Company shall maintain an employee stock option pool equal to 15% of the fully diluted share capital as at Closing, created prior to the investment." Nothing about the headline valuation changed. Meera's stake just fell to 21.49%.

body.text: The pool shuffle is the quietest transfer of value in a term sheet. A pool created before the round comes out of your pocket. A pool created after the round comes out of everyone's, including the new investor's.

children.text: Why Investors Want the Pool Created First

markDefs.definition: An increase in the ESOP pool that is included in the pre-money share count, so the dilution it causes is borne only by the existing shareholders and not by the incoming investor.

children.text: Every growing company needs options to hire with. The argument is not about whether a pool should exist, it is about who pays for it. A

is added to the share count used to calculate the price per share, which lowers that price, which means the investor's rupees buy more of the company. The investor still gets the 25% the term sheet promises, and the enlarged pool is paid for entirely by the people already on the cap table.

columns.label: Pre-money pool (the standard ask)
points: Pool counted in the pre-round share count
Lowers the price per share, so the investor's cheque buys more shares
Existing shareholders absorb 100% of the pool dilution
Investor lands on exactly the percentage the term sheet states

columns.label: Post-money pool (what to push for)
points: Pool created after the round closes
Price per share is unaffected by the top-up
Everyone, including the new investor, is diluted proportionally
Investor ends up slightly below the headline percentage

children.text: TiffinBox goes into the round with 18,750 fully diluted shares, of which 2,000 are the existing pool. That leaves 16,750 shares held by founders, angels, the seed fund and the note holder, and that number cannot change. The investor is putting in ₹6.25 crore for 25%. Watch what the pool line does to everyone else.

body.caption: TiffinBox Series A under three pool treatments (fully diluted)

children.text: Share counts are rounded to whole shares, so percentages can differ in the second decimal place. The structure is what matters. In the pre-money version the investor holds exactly 25% and the founders fall to 35.82% between them. In the post-money version the investor holds 23.10% and the founders keep 36.96%. Same money, same valuation, same pool size, different payer.

body.title: Meera's stake after the Series A under each pool treatment (%)

content.caption: Pre-money pool: solve for the total, because everyone else is squeezed into what is left

children.text: Pre-money version: existing non-pool shares are 16,750 and they must fit into 60% of the company, because the investor takes 25% and the pool takes 15%. Total = 16,750 ÷ 0.60 = 27,916.67, rounded to 27,917 shares. Pool = 4,188 options, investor = 6,979 shares. Meera = 6,000 ÷ 27,917 = 21.49%. The price per share drops to ₹6,25,00,000 ÷ 6,979 = about ₹8,955, down from ₹10,000, which is precisely how the investor gets paid for the pool.

Post-money version: close the round first at 25,000 shares and ₹10,000 per share, then create the pool. Non-pool shares are 23,000 and must fit into 85% of the enlarged company. Total = 23,000 ÷ 0.85 = 27,058.82, rounded to 27,059 shares. Pool = 4,059 options. Meera = 6,000 ÷ 27,059 = 22.17%, and the investor is diluted to 6,250 ÷ 27,059 = 23.10%.

stats.label: Meera's actual fall
stats.context: A third of her stake, not a quarter

stats.label: Price per share effect
stats.context: The investor buys 729 more shares for the same cheque

body.text: Read every term sheet for the words "as at Closing", "prior to the investment" or "on a pre-money basis" near the option pool clause. Those five words decide who pays for the pool. If the clause is silent, assume the investor intends pre-money and ask for it to be spelled out, in writing, before you sign.

children.text: Argue About the Size, Not Just the Timing

Investors ask for 10% to 15% because it is a round number that protects them from a top-up at the next round. The right number is whatever your hiring plan actually needs until the next raise. Build it bottom-up, role by role, and take the plan into the negotiation. A founder with a spreadsheet beats a founder with an opinion.

body.caption: TiffinBox bottom-up pool plan for the 18 months after the round

children.text: TiffinBox needs about 5.45% of new grants, and it already has unallocated options on the cap table. A 15% pool is therefore roughly double what the next 18 months require. The founders are not arguing that employees should get less. They are arguing that options nobody will grant for two years should not be created and paid for today.

body.label: What one point of pool costs you
body.context: In this round, each percentage point of pre-money pool costs the founders roughly 0.60 percentage points of their own ownership, because they hold 10,000 of the 16,750 existing non-pool shares, just under 60%. Work out your own multiplier before the negotiation.

body.text: There are three ways to win this negotiation and you rarely get all three. Ask for the pool to be sized to an actual hiring plan. Ask for it to be created post-money, or at least split between pre-money and post-money. Ask for unallocated options to be returned to the pool and counted, rather than a fresh top-up on top of what is already unused. Pick the two that matter most to your cap table and trade the third.

body.title: Solve for the post-round total
body.prompt: A Pune startup's existing shareholders hold 16,750 shares excluding any option pool. The new investor will hold 25% and the term sheet requires a pre-money pool equal to 15% of the post-round fully diluted capital. How many fully diluted shares will exist after the round? Round to the nearest whole share.
body.explanation: Existing non-pool shares must fit into 100% minus 25% minus 15% = 60% of the company. 16,750 ÷ 0.60 = 27,916.67, so about 27,917 shares. The pool is 4,188 options and the investor receives 6,979 shares.

body.title: Name the timing
body.textWithBlank: An option pool that is included in the share count used to price the round, so that only the existing shareholders are diluted by it, is called a ___-money pool.
body.explanation: A pre-money pool lowers the price per share, so the investor's cheque buys more shares and lands on exactly the headline percentage. A post-money pool dilutes the new investor too.

body.title: Which clause costs you most?
body.question: Four term sheets offer the same ₹10 crore at the same ₹40 crore pre-money valuation. Which option pool clause is worst for the founders?
options: A 10% pool created after the round closes
An 18% pool included in the pre-money share count
A 12% pool created after the round closes
A 10% pool included in the pre-money share count
body.explanation: Two things make a pool clause expensive: how big it is, and whether it sits pre-money. The 18% pre-money pool is both the largest and the one the founders pay for entirely, so it costs them the most. A 12% post-money pool spreads its dilution across everyone, including the new investor.

body.title: Fifteen percent, non-negotiable
body.scenario: You are raising ₹12 crore at ₹48 crore pre-money for your Hyderabad fintech. Your fully diluted cap table has 30,000 shares, including an existing pool of 2,400 options of which 900 are ungranted. The term sheet requires a 15% pool as at Closing, created pre-money. Your 18-month hiring plan needs about 6% in new grants. The partner says the 15% is "standard, we do it in every deal".
body.prompt: What do you propose, and what does each concession get you?
body.modelAnswer:
First, do the arithmetic so you are arguing with numbers. Your existing non-pool shares are 30,000 minus 2,400 = 27,600. The investor takes ₹12 crore ÷ ₹60 crore post-money = 20%. With a 15% pre-money pool, everyone else is squeezed into 65%: total = 27,600 ÷ 0.65 = about 42,462 shares, of which the pool is about 6,369 options and the investor about 8,492 shares.

What to propose, in order of what it is worth to you:
1. Count what already exists. You have 900 ungranted options. A pool defined as 15% of post-round capital should absorb those rather than sit on top of them. Establishing this alone can be worth a full percentage point.
2. Size it to the plan. Take your role-by-role hiring plan to the meeting: about 6% of new grants over 18 months, plus the ungranted 900, supports a pool closer to 9% or 10% than 15%. Offer a contractual commitment to top the pool up if you exceed the plan.
3. Split the timing. If the size will not move, ask that the top-up be split, for example half pre-money and half post-money. This is often easier for an investor to accept than a pure post-money pool because it preserves most of their headline percentage.
4. Trade it deliberately. If the fund genuinely will not move on the pool, ask for something priced elsewhere in exchange: a higher pre-money valuation, a narrower list of reserved matters, or a longer runway through a larger cheque at the same pre-money.

What not to do: accept "it is standard" as an answer. The size and timing of the pool are negotiated in most rounds, and the cost of losing this argument is measured in percentage points of your own company.

body.title: Working the pool clause
steps: Find the pool clause and note the size, and whether it says pre-money, post-money or nothing at all.
Build a bottom-up hiring plan for the period until the next round, role by role, with a grant percentage for each.
Add existing ungranted options and insist they count towards the required pool.
Model your stake three ways: no pool change, the requested pool pre-money, and the same pool post-money.
Work out your own cost multiplier: how much of each pool percentage point comes out of your stake.
Propose a smaller pool sized to the plan, with a commitment to top up later if hiring runs ahead.
If the size is fixed, negotiate the timing, or trade the pool against valuation or governance terms.
Make sure the final agreed pool number and its timing are written into the term sheet in words.

cards.definition: Requiring an enlarged ESOP pool to be created before a round so that existing shareholders alone bear the dilution.
A pool included in the pre-round share count, which lowers the price per share and is paid for by existing holders.
A pool created after the round closes, diluting every holder including the new investor.
An increase in the size of the option pool, usually demanded as a condition of a new round.
Options reserved but not yet granted. They should count towards any required pool size.
An additional option grant to an existing employee, often given as earlier grants approach full vesting.
Sizing a pool by listing the roles to be hired and the grant each will need, rather than accepting a round number.

points: The option pool clause can cost a founder more than the headline dilution, and it is easy to miss.
A pre-money pool is included in the pricing share count, lowers the price per share and is paid for entirely by existing shareholders.
A post-money pool dilutes everyone proportionally, including the new investor.
At TiffinBox, a 15% pre-money pool takes Meera to 21.49% instead of 22.17% post-money, and the founders to 35.82% instead of 36.96%.
Headline dilution of 25% became an actual fall of roughly a third of Meera's stake, from 32.00% to 21.49%.
Size the pool bottom-up from a real hiring plan, and insist that existing ungranted options count towards it.
If you cannot win the size, negotiate the timing, split it, or trade it against valuation and governance terms.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other startups described are fictional, and all valuations, share counts, grant sizes and percentages are illustrative rather than benchmarks. Share counts have been rounded to whole shares, so percentages may differ slightly in the second decimal place. Consult a qualified company secretary, chartered accountant or lawyer before negotiating or closing a fundraise.
